current.rappels: 2-3 rappels with a single 60 m rope through the Great Chimney and the snow gully; parties on shorter ropes report 4-5
current.rappel_count_note: Accounts disagree on the count. One party made three rappels on the way down; another needed just two, starting at the top of the keyhole, to get down. A third account describes five rappels, but that is one party’s descent on two 25 m ropes rather than a list of fixed stations — which is why its lengths (about 23 m / 75 ft) look so precise and why its count disagrees with the others. That party’s final rappel off the southeast rib jammed and they sacrificed a rope; the standard line threads the low keyhole beneath the chockstone for a cleaner pull.

rappel_detail.notes: First rappel off the upper south saddle down the slabby trough, before reaching the Great Chimney.

rappel_detail.pull: About 75 ft of drop, so a 60 m rope doubled covers it. A party on 25 m ropes was left roughly five metres short and had to break the chimney into two rappels.
rappel_detail.notes: 75-ft rappel through the Great Chimney cannonhole (a narrow squeeze slot).
hazards: The tunnel is a real squeeze — packs come off and get pushed through ahead of you, which is exactly why parties take the lip instead
Going over the lip loads the chockstone edge: a block there has split under rope tension and run down the chimney, striking both climbers of one party
Anchors through the chimney are aged natural slings, described by more than one party as questionable, and the chimney funnels everything that comes loose
rappel_detail.station: The highest chockstone in the Great Chimney. There are two ways to rig it: through the low keyhole/tunnel under the chockstone, which is the recommended line and gives a low-angle drop, or over the lip of the chockstone, which is overhanging.

rappel_detail.notes: 75-ft rappel off a mid-chimney chockstone, ending at a narrow ledge; party then traverses back to the high southeast notch.
hazards: The landing is a narrow exposed ledge, not easy ground, and it is where the descent changes direction
Anything dislodged in the chimney runs a long way; parties on this face have sent rock all the way down to the glacier below
rappel_detail.station: A slung chockstone partway down the chimney. The rappel ends on a narrow, exposed ledge — from there parties traverse back to the high southeast notch rather than continuing straight down the chimney line.

rappel_detail.notes: Rappel down the snow/rock gully, passing through a snow cannonhole halfway down.
hazards: Moats are open on both sides of the snow fin at the hole
rappel_detail.station: Rappel down the snow/rock gully from the high southeast notch. Halfway down the line threads a second cannonhole — this one a hole through a tall snow fin.

rappel_detail.pull: Pull from as far out of the cleft as the ground allows, and treat a spare cord or a stuck-rope plan as part of the rack rather than optional.
rappel_detail.notes: Final rappel through a rock cleft on the southeast rib back to descent terrain; ropes are prone to sticking here (one party sacrificed a rope).
hazards: This is the documented rope-eater on the route: a party's rope jammed on the pull here, resisted every retrieval attempt, and was left on the mountain — in the dark, on the way out
rappel_detail.station: The final rappel drops through a cleft in the rock of the southeast rib back onto walking terrain.

current.descent_text: Descend by reversing the Southeast Face/South Ridge line back down to the South AmBo Saddle — the terrain is loose and complex enough that there is no clean walk-off alternative. Expect two to four short rappels through the summit chimney/gully system, with the count depending on party size, rope handling, and which chockstone squeeze you take: the standard, recommended line threads the low "keyhole"/tunnel beneath a large chockstone (pull packs off, push them through, crawl after), giving a clean, low-angle rappel; parties who instead rig over the lip of the chockstone get a harder, overhanging drop and sometimes add an extra rappel to manage it. A single 60m rope, doubled, is sufficient for the individual rappels (each reported at around 75 ft/~23 m), so plan on doubled-strand rappels off a 60m rope rather than needing two ropes. Anchors are entirely natural — slung chockstones and horns with in-place webbing that is often sun-bleached and aged — there are no bolts on this route, so inspect and back up (or replace) any tat you find and carry your own cord/rap rings; at least one party describes sacrificing a rope that got stuck in a rappel crack, so a pull-cord or a stuck-rope contingency is worth planning for. After the last rappel off the southeast rib, downclimb loose 3rd-class terrain back into the red talus bowl, then reverse the long sidehill traverse below Mt. Larrabee back to Gargett Mine and High Pass, and finish on the High Pass Trail to Twin Lakes. Loose rock remains the dominant hazard for the entire descent — keep the party tight through the gullies and budget real time for the tedious traverse back across scree and heather, especially late in the day; parties camped at Gargett Basin typically descend only as far as camp the first evening and walk out to the trailhead the next morning.

current.rappels: One rappel of about 50 ft at the chockstone cleft near the top of the South Gully (or downclimb it on belay), then descend the gully on foot
current.rappel_count_note: The rappels into the notch are two single-rope rappels, or one on a double rope; their lengths and anchors are not recorded. The descent gully adds one short rappel or belayed downclimb at its chockstone step.

rappel_detail.notes: The one rappel of the descent; it can also be downclimbed on belay. A 40 m rope is ideal and a 30 m reaches. Below it, descend the long gully.
rappel_detail.anchor: webbing/sling anchor just above the chockstone (heavily used; back it up)
hazards: The rope can catch on the chockstone on the pull, and you can pendulum if you rappel off to one side.
rappel_detail.station: The short, blocky cleft capped by a chockstone near the top of the South Gully, about 50 ft high.

current.descent_text: From the true summit, scramble back east along the summit ridge to the top of the South Gully. Its one technical step is a short, blocky rock cleft capped by a chockstone, with a fixed sling above it: rappel it or downclimb it on belay. Below that, descend the long gully and the brushy, forested slope beneath it toward Ingalls Creek, return to camp, and reverse the approach over Fourth Creek Pass to the trailhead. The descent is long, so leave the summit with a comfortable margin of daylight.

current.rappels: 3 single-rope rappels, sometimes 4: one from the upper rock band to a ledge on the southeast face, then two or three more in the gully immediately east of the top of the Northeast Couloir, down to the snow. Anchors are natural and may need rigging. Some parties instead make two rappels down slabs north of the east gully and traverse a wet ledge into it.
current.rappel_count_note: The stations follow the usual descent: one rappel to the southeast-face ledge, then down the gully east of the couloir’s top, where two or three single-rope rappels reach the snow, so 3-4 rappels in all. Anchors are natural and not guaranteed to be in place; carry webbing and nuts. The other line, two rappels down slabs north of the east gully off slung blocks and a small tree, then a protected wet-ledge traverse into the gully, is an alternative, not a continuation.

rappel_detail.notes: This table follows the southeast-face ledge line. The other descent involves two rappels on the slabs directly north of the east gully, followed by a traverse along a wet ledge into it. Choose one line before you leave the summit.
rappel_detail.anchor: Natural, and not guaranteed to be in place — you may need to rig the anchor yourself, and one earlier party describes rappelling off a tree with a sling, on the ledge facing southeast. Carry webbing and nuts for this descent.
hazards: No reliable fixed station — arriving expecting one and finding nothing is the failure mode here
You are committing off the summit onto a face on the opposite side of the peak from the couloir you climbed
rappel_detail.station: Head back down from the summit to the upper rock band; the single rappel from there drops onto the ledge on the southeast face.

rappel_detail.anchor: Natural / rigged; an older two-rope description set up at a stopper anchor midway up the southeast face.
hazards: Anchors may have to be built from nuts and left behind
rappel_detail.station: First of the rappels down the gully lying east of the top of the Northeast Couloir, entered from the southeast-face ledge.

rappel_detail.notes: A third rappel in this gully is described as sometimes necessary, so treat the count as two or three here rather than fixed.
hazards: Loose gully; the transition onto snow at the bottom may need axe and crampons depending on season
rappel_detail.station: Continues down the same gully; the sequence ends on the snow slopes below, from which parties traverse toward the Colchuck-Dragontail notch or glissade the Colchuck Glacier.

current.descent_text: Retrace your steps from the summit to the upper rock band, then make one rappel onto the ledge on the southeast face; you may need to rig a natural anchor, and one party used a slung tree there. Then head over to the top of the Northeast Couloir and find the gully just east of it: two or three single-rope rappels down that gully reach the snow slopes below. Anchors are natural and not reliably in place, so carry webbing and nuts to build them. Alternatively, some parties make two rappels on the slabs immediately north of the east gully, off slings around blocks and a small tree, then traverse a wet, snow-covered ledge into the gully. Either way, finish with a roughly 2,500 ft glissade down the Colchuck Glacier to the lake, then out via the Colchuck Lake trail. Another option drops via a different gully into Porcupine Creek Basin with a traverse around Colchuck Peak.

current.rappels: 3 single-rope rappels off the summit block (a single 50m rope reaches; a 60m or two 50m ropes are more comfortable for parties of 3+)

rappel_detail.notes: First of three single-rope rappels (a single 50m rope is sufficient) down the west side of the summit block toward the ridge notch. This is the only reasonable retreat once on the roped summit block — there is no walk-off partway up.
rappel_detail.anchor: rock station on the west side of the summit block (anchor type not recorded)

rappel_detail.notes: Second of the three single-rope rappels; route-finding through the ledges on this descent is reported as the crux, slower than the ascent.
rappel_detail.anchor: rock station on the summit block (anchor type not recorded)

rappel_detail.notes: Final rappel reaching the ridge notch; from there downclimb the Class 3-4 gully system back to the base of the face and retrace through Dutch Miller Gap.
rappel_detail.anchor: rock station on the summit block (anchor type not recorded)

current.descent_text: From the summit, make three single-rope rappels (a single 50m rope is sufficient) down the west side of the summit block to the ridge notch, then downclimb the Class 3-4 gully system back to the base of the face. Route-finding through the ledges is the crux of the descent and is reported to be slower than the ascent (~4.7 hrs summit-to-camp vs. ~6.0 hrs camp-to-summit). Retrace the approach through Dutch Miller Gap and the Middle Fork trail back to the trailhead.

current.rappels: 1 long rappel (reported as about 60 m) from a notch on the south ridge, then about two rope-lengths of steep downclimbing to the lower basin

rappel_detail.notes: One long rappel, reported as roughly 60 m; some parties found a 60 m rope barely reaches the anchor. Below it, bypass steep snow and waterfall-wet rock to the side and downclimb about two more rope-lengths of steep terrain to the lower basin.
hazards: Check that your rope reaches before committing.
In winter and spring parties downclimb the Dry Creek couloir instead, which is insecure and dangerous.
rappel_detail.station: A notch on the south ridge, reached by reversing the summit ridge over the lower first bump.

current.descent_text: Most parties descend the same Dry Creek line they climbed. From the true summit, reverse the summit ridge over the lower (first) bump, then set up a roughly 60-meter rappel from a notch on the south ridge -- some parties have found a 60m rope barely reaches the anchor/chockstone. Below the rappel, bypass steep snow and waterfall-moistened rock to the side, then downclimb roughly two more rope-lengths of steep terrain to regain the lower basin before retracing the approach back across the South Fork Stillaguamish and out to the trailhead. In winter/spring, parties instead downclimb the Dry Creek couloir itself, which parties describe as a genuinely dangerous, insecure downclimb.

current.rappels: Descend the West Route gully: one single-rope rappel from slung blocks at the notch. Rappelling Beckey-Tate itself takes five or six two-rope rappels off slings and trees through loose rock, and most parties avoid it.

rappel_detail.notes: The one rappel, on a single 60 m rope, below the steepest, loosest part of the gully. Some parties split it into two using an intermediate anchor lower down.
rappel_detail.anchor: slung block at the notch (two tat anchors to choose from)
hazards: Tat anchors: inspect and back up. The gully is loose.
rappel_detail.station: The belay notch below the summit slab, after downclimbing or top-roping the leader off the summit; there is no anchor on the summit itself.

current.descent_text: Do not plan to rappel the Beckey-Tate line itself — while it's technically possible with two ropes (roughly five or six rappels off slings and trees), the route wanders and holds a lot of large loose rock, making rope-stuck and rockfall risk high; most parties explicitly avoid it. Instead, from the top of the route scramble about 20 ft up and left to reach the notch that separates the south face from the true summit, which stands a few hundred feet higher. To tag it, drop about 150 ft of scree on the far side, cross north into the West Route gully and climb its short pitches to the unprotected 5.6 summit slab (protected by a single old bolt), which is downclimbed or top-roped; then descend the shared gully: two slung-block anchors get you down with one or two single-rope rappels (a 60m rope is sufficient either way) through the steep/loose upper gully, after which it's a scree-and-snow walk/glissade down the gully back to the approach basin, across Early Winters Creek, and out the climbers' trail to the Hairpin Turn. Expect the full descent to take a couple of hours; keep helmets on throughout given the loose rock in the gully.

current.rappels: Two ~200-ft rappels down slabs on the standard descent

rappel_detail.notes: First of two ~200 ft rappels down steep slabs on the West Peak's northwest side; a rope of at least 60m (or two ropes joined) is needed to reach the next stance.
rappel_detail.anchor: gear anchor (nut, per one documented descent)

rappel_detail.notes: Second ~200 ft rappel reaching the approach basin; anchors here are improvised rather than fixed, so carry a small rack/cordage. Some parties finish this descent after dark.
rappel_detail.anchor: gear anchor (piton, per one documented descent)

current.descent_text: From the Southwest Peak (route's high point), traverse the Northeast Ridge to the West Peak — about 2 hours, negotiating a series of gendarmes mostly on 3rd/4th-class ledges, with one short rappel along the way. From the West Peak, descend the northwest side: downclimb talus, then make two rappels of roughly 200 feet each down steep slabs back into the approach basin. Anchors on this descent have historically been improvised rather than fixed — one documented descent used a nut at the top station and a piton at the lower one — so carry a small rack/cordage to build or reinforce anchors rather than counting on hardware being in place. Two 200-ft rappels require a rope of at least 60m (or two ropes joined) to reach each next stance without coming up short. Parties have finished this descent after dark on long summit days, so budget extra time and bring a headlamp. From the bottom of the raps, continue downclimbing talus back to camp near the 7,100' pass, then reverse the terrace descent to Hart Lake and the Railroad Creek Trail back to Holden.
